overhead.method: An open-loop load generator in the benchmark process sends each scenario to the mock provider directly and through the gateway (each in its own process, loopback). The mock answers after a fixed 100 ms time to first token and streams 500 tokens at 2000 tokens/s. Each stream is one keep-alive connection, opened before the run, with its own schedule of evenly spaced send times (5 requests/s non-streaming, 1.25 requests/s streaming) starting at a seeded random phase, so connections do not fire together; a request still running at the next scheduled time delays the next one, and client-side latency always counts from the scheduled time (coordinated omission included). Added TTFB is the gateway's own per-request measure from its traces (`addedTtfbMs`: from the start of request handling to forwarding upstream, with a sub-millisecond clock in the benchmark), so it is paired per request; it does not include time a request waits before the gateway starts handling it, nor the response path. The client-side columns are absolute percentiles of each path, never subtracted from each other; "outside the provider" is each request's TTFB minus the mock's own wait for that request (the `x-mock-wait-ms` header), paired per request, so the mock's timer jitter drops out. An added TTFB SLO row is met only when both the gateway-measured value and the client-side TTFB outside the provider through the gateway (an upper bound on what the gateway adds, which includes queueing before handling) are under target. Each scenario runs at 1, 10, 16, 64, 100, 256, 500 streams; 10, 100, 500 back the SLO rows (about 2,200 scheduled requests each), the other levels about 300. Throughput is answered (2xx) requests and output tokens per second of each run, from its first scheduled send to its last answer (direct: the mock's fixed output per answer; through the gateway: the output tokens its traces settled); at a fixed open-loop rate it follows the offered load until a path saturates, then falls below it. n is the number of samples behind each percentile. CPU is the gateway process's user plus system time over the run's wall time (100% is one core); RSS growth is its peak during the run above its size just before it; per 100 streams is the slope between 100 and 500 streams. The gateway runs examples/policy with every budget level enforced at a limit the load never reaches, no rate limits, guardrails on, traces written and metrics kept.

headroom.note: session-aware reserves the same as worst-case here: the estimator is not given the session's previous cache read share yet (src/policy/decide.ts passes none), and the route sets no reserveOutputTokens.

cache.note: The naive proxy flattens `system` into a string, which drops the cache breakpoint on the system block. This session also marks the newest user block, and that breakpoint caches the whole prefix, the flattened system text included, so through the naive proxy the session still reads almost the same prefix from cache and costs about the same; its usage still differs from the direct run (conformance test C15b fails on it).

soak.method: The shipped bundle (bin/tokenyard.mjs serve, policy from a directory, traces written, ops listener on) runs under an open-loop load with Poisson arrivals against the mock providers on loopback: Claude Code main turns (streaming, growing cached context), subagents, auxiliary and compaction calls, Codex Responses (streaming and not), product traffic with PII, client aborts mid-stream, secret blocks with session taint, refused models, hostile attribution headers (up to 900 characters of quotes, braces, percent signs and Latin-1 on every attribution header, new on every request; session ids from a fixed set of 300 such values), upstream 500, 529, mid-stream errors and dropped connections, a noisy key over its rate and stream limits every minute and 24 requests with max_tokens 128,000 and a 1.1 MB body at once on one session every two minutes, over the enforced 200 USD session budget. New sessions cycle through a fixed set of ids per key, because each distinct session id holds counter state for 30 days by design; that cost is measured on its own (Redis keys and bytes per key). A preloaded probe (bench/soak-probe.mjs; the bundle is unchanged) reports every 30 s the event loop delay since the previous sample, then RSS and heap used right after a full GC (--expose-gc), and active handles; lsof gives open descriptors and TCP sockets; /metrics gives the series count and open reservations; the trace directory gives files and bytes; Redis gives keys by class and used memory. Memory is judged after a 5 minute warm-up: the least-squares trend over the rest of the run, projected over it, and the last 5 minutes against the first 5 must each stay under 10%. Descriptors, sockets and handles are compared idle before and after the load. After the load every key must admit its full concurrent stream limit at once with one more refused, no reservation may be open or left to the sweeper, and in Redis no reservation, deadline or stream count may remain.
